'''''Dracaena reflexa''''' (commonly called '''song of India'''<ref name=GRIN/> or '''song of Jamaica''') is a tree native to [[Mozambique]], [[Madagascar]], [[Mauritius]], and other nearby islands of the Indian Ocean.{{R|POWO}} It is widely grown as an ornamental plant and houseplant, valued for its richly coloured, evergreen leaves, and thick, irregular stems.

==Description==
While it may reach a height of 4–5 m, rarely 6 m in ideal, protected locations, ''D. reflexa'' is usually much smaller, especially when grown as a houseplant. It is slow-growing and upright in habit, tending to an oval shape. The lanceolate leaves are simple, spirally arranged, 5–20 cm long and 1.5–5 cm broad at the base, with a parallel venation and entire margin; they grow in tight whorls and are a uniform dark green.<ref>Huxley, A., ed. (1992). ''New RHS Dictionary of Gardening''. Macmillan.</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=Gilman, E. F. |year=1999 |title=Fact Sheet FPS-187: Dracaena reflexa |publisher=Environmental Horticulture Department, Florida Cooperative Extension Service, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida |url=http://hort.ufl.edu/shrubs/DRAREFA.PDF |access-date=2006-04-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061101053201/http://hort.ufl.edu/shrubs/DRAREFA.PDF |archive-date=2006-11-01 }}</ref>

The flowers are small, clustered, usually white and extremely fragrant, appearing in mid winter. Neither the flowers nor the fruit are especially showy. ''D. reflexa'' var. ''angustifolia'' (syn. ''D. marginata'') differs in having a magenta tint to its flowers, a shrubby habit, and olive green leaves.<ref>Missouri Botanical Garden. Dracaena reflexa var. angustifolia Baker. Conspectus of the Vascular Plants of Madagascar. Retrieved April 18, 2006 from {{cite web|url=http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/Madagasc/liliac/00615149.html |title=Dracaena reflexa var. Angustifolia Baker |access-date=2006-04-18 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303171927/http://www.mobot.org/MOBOT/Madagasc/liliac/00615149.html |archive-date=2016-03-03 }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Dracaena reflexa'' was first described by [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] in 1786. It has been placed in several other related genera, including ''[[Cordyline]]'' and ''Pleomele''.{{R|POWO}}

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Dracaena reflexaSong of Jamaica1.jpg|thumb|upright|''Dracaena reflexa'': Song of Jamaica]]
[[File:Reflex Dracaena.JPG|thumb|right|Specimen at [[North Carolina Zoo]]]]
''Dracaena reflexa'' is a popular ornamental plant, both in the landscape and the home. It can be enjoyed as a specimen plant, accent, or pruned to create a border. Several [[cultivar]]s have been selected, particularly [[variegation|variegated]] clones with cream and yellow-green margins. It performs well as a houseplant, tolerating infrequent waterings. It prefers bright, filtered light, without direct sun exposure, restricted outdoors to [[hardiness zone|zones]] 10–11. It has average water needs and should be [[fertilizer|fertilized]] bi-weekly when actively growing. Although it can survive in relatively low light levels, the plant may grow spindly if given insufficient light. When grown indoors, temperatures of {{convert|18|to|25|C|F}} should be maintained. It can be propagated via herbaceous stem cuttings.{{citation needed|date=April 2018}}

The cultivar ''Dracaena reflexa'' 'Variegata'  has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/102124/i-Dracaena-reflexa-i-Variegata-(v)/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Dracaena reflexa'' 'Variegata'
| access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref> (confirmed 2017)<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 33 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 24 January 2018}}</ref>

Traditional medicine practitioners of Madagascar have long believed ''Dracaena reflexa'' to cure [[malaria]]l symptoms, poisoning, [[dysentery]], [[diarrhea]], [[dysmenorrhea]], and to be useful as an [[antipyretic]] and [[hemostatic]] agent. The leaves and bark are mixed with parts of a number of other native plants and mixed into herbal teas. Its effectiveness in any such treatment remains unproven.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Randrianarivelojosia | first1 = R. | display-authors = etal | year = 2003 | title = Plants traditionally prescribed to treat tazo (malaria) in the eastern region of Madagascar | journal = Malaria Journal | volume = 2 | article-number = 25 | pmc=184444 | pmid=12921540 | doi=10.1186/1475-2875-2-25 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

[[File:Dracaena reflexaSong of India1.jpg|thumb|right|''Dracaena reflexa'': Song of India]]The fruit of ''D. reflexa'' is also important to the diet of the [[Madagascar|Malagasy]] [[black-and-white ruffed lemur]] (''Varecia variegata variegata'').<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Britt | first1 = A | year = 2000 | title = Diet and feeding behaviour of the Black-and-White Ruffed Lemur (''Varecia variegata variegata'') in the Betampona Reserve, eastern Madagascar | journal = Folia Primatologica | volume = 71 | issue = 3| pages = 133–141 | doi=10.1159/000021741| pmid = 10828690 | s2cid = 11002097 }}</ref> The [[Frégate beetle]] (''Polposipus herculeanus''), an endangered species endemic to [[Frégate Island]] in the Seychelles, is also known to associate with this plant.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ferguson |first1=A. |last2=Pearce-Kelly |first2=P. |name-list-style=amp |year=2005 |title=Captive management of the Frégate Island giant tenebrionid beetle ''Polposipus herculeanus'' |journal=Phelsuma |volume=13 |pages=25–43 |doi= |url=https://islandbiodiversity.com/Phelsuma%2013-2.pdf }}</ref>

==''Dracaena reflexa'' var. ''angustifolia''==
[[File:Roots of Dracaena marginata 'Tricolor'.jpg|thumb|Roots of ''Dracaena reflexa'' var. ''angustifolia'' (''Dracaena marginata 'Tricolor''')]]
[[File:Dracaena marginata 11zz.jpg|thumb|''Dracaena tricolor'']]
''Dracaena reflexa'' var. ''angustifolia'' is also known as ''D. marginata'', a name found in horticulture.{{R|POWO2}} This is a durable popular tropical house plant from Madagascar. The thin leaves are linear and a deep, glossy green color with red edges; typically 30–90 cm long and 2–7 cm broad, tapering to an acuminate point. It is a popular houseplant that needs little attention, with several [[cultivar]]s available with the leaves [[Variegation|variegated]] with red or pale yellow.

It requires a minimum temperature of {{convert|15|°C|°F|abbr=on}}, and is more tolerant than most plants of dry soil and irregular watering, though liable to root decay in permanently wet soil. Because it requires minimal care it is very popular in offices where the constant heat and light suits its growing requirements. They can grow between 2.5–4 meters in height and will ultimately spread between 1.5 and 2.5 meters.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/31916/Dracaena-marginata-(v)/Details|title=RHS (Royal Horticultural Society)|date=November 2017}}</ref>

There are many commonly used names to describe this variety that arise due to the various growth patterns and different cultivars. Some of the most popular are red edge dracaena, Madagascar dragon tree dracaena, dragon blood tree, and tree dracaena.<ref name=":0" /> With the variety of forms and cultivars, there are also some [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid crosses]] that can arise as well.

The cultivar 'Tricolor' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/106994/Dracaena-marginata-Tricolor-(v)/Details | title = ''Dracaena marginata'' 'Tricolor' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 May 2020}}</ref>

===Versatility===
The plant can be grown in virtually any pattern, with the most popular being bush, straight cane, staggered cane, tree form, and custom character forms. The variety also has a handful of different cultivars from [[selective breeding]]. These include 'Tarzan', 'Magenta', 'Tricolor', and 'Colorama'.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://plantcaretoday.com/care-dracaena-marginata.html|title=Dracaena Marginata Care: Growing The Red Edged Madagascar Dragon Tree|date=2017-09-01|work=Plant Care Today|access-date=2017-09-22|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Uses===
It is one of the plants used in the [[NASA Clean Air Study]] and has shown to help remove [[formaldehyde]].{{citation needed|date=January 2026}} It is an effective air cleaner and is said to be among the best plants for removing [[xylene]] and [[trichloroethylene]].<ref>{{cite book|title=How to Grow Fresh Air|author=Wolverton, B.C.|publisher=[[Penguin Books]]|year=1996|isbn=0-14-026243-1|location=New York|page=72}}</ref>
